_meta.purpose: MATEL TTP mapping evidence base. Every row is a technique asserted by the cited authority.
_meta.evidence_class: Documented = stated on the MITRE software/group page or in the advisory text; Reported = attributed via the group's technique list sourcing vendor reporting; Inferred = analyst synthesis with no direct single-source sentence.
_meta.note: MITRE ATT&CK Enterprise technique identifiers as published 2026.

TA505.alias: Hive0065, Spandex Tempest, CHIMBORAZO, Evil Corp overlap

FIN6.alias: Skeleton Spider, ITG08, Gold Franklin, Magecart Group 6, TAAL, Camouflage Tempest

ttp.evidence: Emotet has been delivered by phishing emails containing attachments.
Emotet has been delivered by phishing emails containing links.
Emotet has relied upon users clicking on a malicious link delivered through spearphishing.
Emotet has relied upon users clicking on a malicious attachment delivered through spearphishing.

ttp.technique: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic
ttp.evidence: Emotet has sent Microsoft Word documents with embedded macros that will invoke scripts to download additional payloads.
Emotet has used PowerShell to retrieve the malicious payload and download additional resources such as Mimikatz.
Emotet has used WMI to execute powershell.exe.

ttp.technique: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
ttp.evidence: Emotet has been observed adding the downloaded payload to HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run.

ttp.technique: Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service
ttp.evidence: Emotet has been observed creating new services to maintain persistence.
Emotet has maintained persistence through a scheduled task, e.g. through a .dll file in the Registry.

ttp.technique: Obfuscated Files or Information: Software Packing
ttp.evidence: Emotet has used custom packers to protect its payloads.

ttp.technique: Obfuscated Files or Information: Binary Padding
ttp.evidence: Emotet inflates malicious files and malware as an evasion technique.
Emotet uses RegSvr32 to execute the DLL payload.
Emotet uses a copy of certutil.exe stored in a temporary directory for process hollowing.
Emotet installed itself as service name 'Windows Defender System Service' with display name 'WinDefService'.

ttp.technique: Credentials from Password Stores: Credentials from Web Browsers
ttp.evidence: Emotet has been observed dropping browser password grabber modules.
Emotet has been observed dropping and executing password grabber modules including Mimikatz.
Emotet has enumerated non-hidden network shares using WNetEnumResourceW.

ttp.technique: System Network Configuration Discovery: Wi-Fi Discovery
ttp.evidence: Emotet can extract names of all locally reachable Wi-Fi networks and brute-force them to spread.
Emotet has leveraged the Admin$, C$, and IPC$ shares for lateral movement.
Emotet has been seen exploiting SMB via EternalBlue (MS17-010) to achieve lateral movement and propagation.
Emotet has used HTTP for command and control.
Emotet has used HTTP over ports such as 20, 22, 443, 7080 and 50000.
Emotet is known to use RSA keys for encrypting C2 traffic; data is encrypted before sending to the C2 server.
Emotet has used Google Protobufs to serialize C2 data and Base64 to encode data before sending to the C2 server.
Emotet has exfiltrated data over its C2 channel.
TA505 has registered domains to impersonate services such as Dropbox to distribute malware.
TA505 has used AdFind, BloodHound, Mimikatz and PowerSploit in their operations.
TA505 has used spearphishing emails with malicious attachments to initially compromise victims.
TA505 has sent spearphishing emails containing malicious links.
TA505 has used lures to get users to enable content in malicious attachments and execute malicious files contained in archives.

ttp.technique: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic
ttp.evidence: TA505 has used VBS for code execution.
TA505 has used JavaScript for code execution.
TA505 has used PowerShell to download and execute malware and reconnaissance scripts.
TA505 has leveraged rundll32.exe to execute malicious DLLs.
TA505 has used msiexec to download and execute malicious Windows Installer files.
TA505 has signed payloads with code signing certificates from Thawte and Sectigo.

ttp.technique: Obfuscated Files or Information: Software Packing
ttp.evidence: TA505 has used UPX to obscure malicious code.
TA505 has used malware to disable Windows Defender.

ttp.technique: Credentials from Password Stores: Credentials from Web Browsers
ttp.evidence: TA505 has used malware to gather credentials from Internet Explorer.
TA505 has used malware to gather credentials from FTP clients and Outlook.
TA505 has used TinyMet to enumerate members of privileged groups and has run 'net group /domain'.
TA505 has used stolen domain admin accounts to compromise additional hosts.
TA505 has used HTTP to communicate with C2 nodes.
TA505 has used fast flux to mask botnets by distributing payloads across multiple IPs.
Dridex contains a backconnect module for tunneling traffic through a victim; infected computers join a P2P botnet relaying C2 traffic.
Dridex has encrypted traffic with RC4.
TA505 has used ransomware such as Clop, Locky, Jaff, Bart, Philadelphia and GlobeImposter to encrypt victim files.
FIN6 has used fake job advertisements sent via LinkedIn to spearphish targets.
FIN6 has targeted victims with e-mails containing malicious attachments.
FIN6 has used malicious documents to lure victims into allowing execution of PowerShell scripts.
FIN6 has used PowerShell to gain access to merchant networks and to download and execute shellcode.
FIN6 has used WMI to automate the remote execution of PowerShell scripts.

ttp.technique: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
ttp.evidence: FIN6 has used Registry Run keys to establish persistence for its downloader tools HARDTACK and SHIPBREAD.
FIN6 has used scheduled tasks to establish persistence for HARDTACK, SHIPBREAD and FrameworkPOS.
FIN6 tools targeted CVE-2013-3660, CVE-2011-2005 and CVE-2010-4398 to reach kernel-level privileges.
FIN6 renamed the psexec service name to 'mstdc' to masquerade as a legitimate Windows service.
FIN6 has removed files from victim machines.
FIN6 has used Windows Credential Editor for credential dumping.
FIN6 used Metasploit's PsExec NTDSGRAB module to obtain a copy of the Active Directory database.
FIN6 used publicly available tools including osql.exe to map the internal network and reconnoitre AD, SQL servers and NetBIOS.
FIN6 mapped the internal network and conducted reconnaissance against Active Directory, SQL servers and NetBIOS.
FIN6 used RDP to move laterally in victim networks.
To move laterally, FIN6 used credentials stolen from various systems on which it gathered usernames and password hashes.
FIN6 has collected and exfiltrated payment card data from compromised systems.
FIN6 used a script to iterate through compromised PoS systems, copy and remove data to a log file, and bind to the submit-payment button event.
FIN6 used the Plink command-line utility to create SSH tunnels to C2 servers.
FIN6 has used Metasploit Bind and Reverse TCP stagers.
FIN6 has used Pastebin and Google Storage to host content for their operations.

ttp.technique: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol: Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol
ttp.evidence: FIN6 has sent stolen payment card data to remote servers via HTTP POSTs.
